source.title: Towards Understanding Generalization via Analytical Learning Theory
source.authors: Kenji Kawaguchi; Yoshua Bengio; Vikas Verma; L. Kaelbling

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper; its title differs slightly from the provided title. No truncation or garbling is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests a different explicit regularization method, dual-cutout, and reports test error against standard and single-cutout training. It does not test any listed version directly.
record.gate_note: The dual-cutout comparison bears on explicit regularization generally. Results cited from prior work, theoretical bounds, and comparisons of the paper's own method outside this regularization result are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper discusses random-label generalization and derives bounds distinguishing structured from unstructured labels, but does not establish the memorization and held-out accuracy behavior in V1. Its experiments compare cutout methods, which test none of V1–V8. Input or representation sensitivity in its theory is not the magnitude-scaled weight sharpness measured in V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors present analytical learning theory as a complementary, strongly instance-dependent approach and derive dual-cutout, which has lower reported mean test error than standard and single-cutout training on all three datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The empirical method is dual-cutout consistency regularization, compared with standard and single-cutout training; it does not reproduce an intervention in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset changes the reported test errors; dual-cutout has lower reported error than standard and single-cutout on all three datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: With WideResNet28_10 after 300 epochs, single-cutout and dual-cutout lower mean test error relative to standard training on all three datasets. Dual-cutout achieves 2.61%, 17.54%, and 2.06% on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN, respectively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cutout augmentation and dual-cutout consistency regularization can improve image-classification test performance in this training setting.

record.problems: The excerpt reports five trials and standard deviations but does not state significance tests. The reported experiment tests the proposed cutout methods, not dropout or the other listed claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results were left out. Cited results from previous work and the paper's theoretical statements are not experimental rows.

untested.parts: Near-perfect random-label fitting alongside natural-label generalization and chance random-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe. Sections 4.1–4.2 provide different upper bounds, not these outcomes.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Adding or removing dropout, training-set-size dependence, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness as a predictor of generalization gaps and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 values match the record and summarize five trials as mean ± standard deviation. The authors describe a significant margin but report no significance test. Neither the structured/random-label bounds nor the discussions of flatness establish a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of random labels and generalization on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and effects of tuning or optimizer changes.
Large-batch versus small-batch training and recipe adaptations.
Dropout and its interaction with training-set size, data augmentation, and weight decay; the study tests dual-cutout instead.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other measured properties as predictors of the generalization gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.
